Outstretched
owt-strecht'
adj. (extended, reached out; of the arm by which God brought Israel from Egypt — and, in Jeremiah, by which He fought against them)
From out and stretched, rendering Hebrew netuyah, the passive participle of natah, to stretch out. It is joined almost always to zeroa, an arm, or yad, a hand.

Biblical Definition

The phrase is the standing formula for the Exodus. In the confession made at the offering of firstfruits: “And the LORD brought us forth out of Egypt with a mighty hand, and with an outstretched arm, and with great terribleness, and with signs, and with wonders” (Deuteronomy 26:8). Moses uses it in the great rhetorical question about whether any god ever took a nation from the midst of another nation “by a mighty hand, and by a stretched out arm” (Deuteronomy 4:34), and it grounds the fourth commandment in Deuteronomy's version: “remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt, and that the LORD thy God brought thee out thence through a mighty hand and by a stretched out arm: therefore the LORD thy God commanded thee to keep the sabbath day” (Deuteronomy 5:15). Then Jeremiah turns the formula against the nation, and the reversal is deliberate and terrible: “And I myself will fight against you with an outstretched hand and with a strong arm, even in anger, and in fury, and in great wrath” (Jeremiah 21:5). The same arm, the same vocabulary, aimed the other way. Jeremiah also uses it of creation and of God's right to dispose of the nations (Jeremiah 27:5).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines outstretched as extended, spread out, and stretch as to extend, to reach forth, to exert to the utmost.

expand to see more

OUTSTRETCHED, pp. Extended; stretched out; expanded.

STRETCH, v.t. To draw out to greater length; to extend in a line.

2. To extend in breadth; to spread.

3. To reach out; to extend; as, to stretch out the arm.

ARM, n. Figuratively, power, might; as the secular arm; the arm of the LORD.

Key Scripture

Deuteronomy 26:8 — "And the LORD brought us forth out of Egypt with a mighty hand, and with an outstretched arm, and with great terribleness, and with signs, and with wonders:"

Deuteronomy 5:15 — "And remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt, and that the LORD thy God brought thee out thence through a mighty hand and by a stretched out arm: therefore the LORD thy God commanded thee to keep the sabbath day."

Jeremiah 21:5 — "And I myself will fight against you with an outstretched hand and with a strong arm, even in anger, and in fury, and in great wrath."

Jeremiah 27:5 — "I have made the earth, the man and the beast that are upon the ground, by my great power and by my outstretched arm, and have given it unto whom it seemed meet unto me."

Modern Corruption

God's power is assumed to be permanently on one side, and Jeremiah records the formula of deliverance turned against the delivered.

expand to see more

Jeremiah 21:5 is one of the most alarming verses in the prophets precisely because of its vocabulary. Every Israelite knew an outstretched hand and a strong arm; it was the language of the Exodus, recited at the firstfruits and attached to the sabbath commandment. Jeremiah takes the formula and puts it in God's mouth as a declaration of war against Jerusalem. A people may possess a true history of divine deliverance and find the same power arrayed against them, and no covenant privilege prevents it. Every nation and church that assumes God's arm is permanently committed to its side because of what He did in an earlier generation should read this verse slowly.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the way Deuteronomy grounds obedience. The sabbath command in Deuteronomy 5 is not argued from utility or from need for rest; it is argued from redemption — remember that thou wast a servant… therefore the LORD thy God commanded thee. That is the structure of biblical ethics throughout: the indicative of what God has done, then the imperative of what His people are to do. Preaching that issues commands without rehearsing the deliverance produces moralism, and preaching that rehearses the deliverance and never issues commands produces sentiment. Deuteronomy 5:15 does both in one sentence.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew natah, to stretch out — the participle netuyah in Deuteronomy 4:34, 5:15, 26:8, Jeremiah 21:5, 27:5; joined to zeroa, an arm, and yad chazaqah, a mighty hand.

expand to see more

Hebrew natah — to stretch out, extend; its participle gives the standing formula of the Exodus.

Hebrew zeroa — an arm, and figuratively strength; Deuteronomy 26:8, Isaiah 53:1 of the arm of the LORD revealed.

Hebrew yad chazaqah — a mighty hand; the constant companion of the outstretched arm.

Hebrew mora gadol — great terribleness; Deuteronomy 26:8, one of the five terms in the confession.

Isaiah 53:1 asks the question the formula finally answers: to whom is the arm of the LORD revealed?

Usage

"“With a mighty hand, and with an outstretched arm” — the standing formula of the Exodus."

"“Remember that thou wast a servant… therefore the LORD thy God commanded thee”."

"“I myself will fight against you with an outstretched hand” — the same arm, reversed."
